papers.title: Enhancing cortical electrophysiological signatures of sleep overrides ER stress responses in sleep-deprived mice
papers.abstract: Sleep deprivation (SD) triggers characteristic changes in the cortical electroencephalogram (EEG) during waking and sleep, as well as upregulating molecular signatures of neuronal activity, synaptic plasticity, and endoplasmic reticulum (ER) stress. This includes the induction of the unfolded protein response (UPR), the primary marker and adaptive mechanism of ER stress. Yet how cortical neuronal activity during SD contributes to the induction of these molecular signatures remains unknown. Here we investigate whether manipulating cortical activity during SD with a physiological stimulation paradigm (flickering light stimulation, FLS) affects the induction of the UPR. As expected, SD alone upregulated activity-dependent and UPR-related genes in cortex and led to increased EEG slow-wave activity (SWA) during subsequent NREM sleep, an electrophysiological signature of sleep need. Delivering FLS during SD, however, prevented the upregulation of activity- and UPR-related genes while inducing an additional increase in SWA during subsequent sleep. Further analysis of neuronal firing revealed that FLS induced brief neuronal silent (OFF) periods in awake animals during stimulation, thereby shifting cortical activity towards a brain state resembling sleep. These findings suggest that physiological manipulation of cortical activity during waking is sufficient to dissociate molecular signatures of ER stress from electrophysiological markers of sleep pressure. We propose that global sleep wake history and cortical network dynamics differentially regulate activity-dependent transcription and the accumulation of sleep pressure.

The authors conclude that physiological manipulation of cortical activity can dissociate ER-stress molecular signatures from electrophysiological markers of sleep pressure.

papers.title: ppGpp is present in, and functions to regulate sleep of, Drosophila.
papers.abstract: Sleep is essential for animals, and receives inputs from circadian, homeostasis, and environment, yet the mechanisms of sleep regulation remain elusive. Discovery of molecules in living systems and demonstration of their functional roles are pivotal in furthering our understanding of the molecular basis of biology. Here, we report that guanosine-5'-diphosphate, 3'-diphosphate (ppGpp) is present in Drosophila, and plays an important role in regulation of sleep and starvation-induced sleep loss (SISL). ppGpp is detected in germ-free Drosophila and hydrolyzed by an enzyme encoded by the mesh1 gene in Drosophila. Nighttime sleep and SISL were defected in mesh1 mutant flies, and rescued by expression of wildtype Mesh1, but not the enzymatically defective mutant Mesh1E66A. Ectopic expression of RelA, the Escherichia coli synthetase for ppGpp, phenocopied mesh1 knockout mutants, whereas overexpression of Mesh1 resulted in the opposite phenotypes, supporting that ppGpp is both necessary and sufficient in sleep regulation. A chemo connectomic screen followed by genetic intersection experiments implicates the Dilp2 neurons in the pars intercerebralis (PI) brain region as the site of ppGpp function. Our results have thus validated the presence of ppGpp in Drosophila and revealed a physiological role of ppGpp in sleep regulation for the first time.

papers.title: iFLiP: accessible and low-cost lifetime fiber photometry for robust longitudinal and quantitative measurements of neural dynamics
papers.abstract: Fluorescence lifetime measurements overcome the limitation of widely used intensity-based measurements in quantifying tonic activities and longitudinal changes in neural dynamics. However, while lifetime sensors are rapidly emerging, their applications have been limited by the complexity and expense of required hardware and software. Here, we report a simple, low-cost lifetime fiber photometry system, named iFLiP, that uses entirely off-the-shelf products and can be assembled without specialized expertise. We also develop software that enables turn-key operation. The integrated system can accurately monitor lifetime changes at up to 5000 Hz for days. We demonstrate the utility of iFLiP in monitoring the activity of protein kinase A (PKA) in vitro and in vivo, and uncover striatal subregion- and cell-type-specific PKA dynamics elicited by locomotion in mice. Additionally, multi-day continuous measurements in the basal forebrain reveal previously unappreciated PKA activity associated with sleep/wakefulness. Overall, iFLiP may make lifetime measurements broadly accessible in neuroscience research.

papers.title: NED-Net: an annotation-training loop for rodent EEG event detection
papers.abstract: Long-term EEG monitoring is central to rodent epilepsy research, and manual review is laborious because recordings span hundreds to tens of thousands of animal-hours. Published automated detectors perform well on their development datasets but are typically fixed models that may not adapt to another laboratory's electrodes, animals, or noise conditions. We introduce NED-Net, open-source software for training and maintaining seizure detectors. It uses reviewed candidate events as training labels, runs detection live during recording, and retrains as annotations accumulate. A detector trained on one mouse cohort (867 annotated seizures) achieved 93.6% precision in human review of 171 detections. Applied unchanged to a second cohort on the same acquisition system, its detections were mostly seizures (12 of 13 reviewed), but per-animal recall varied substantially (median 10%), with no convulsive reference seizure detected in four of 11 animals. Retraining with annotations from the second cohort raised convulsive recall from 15% to 64%, with at least one reference seizure detected in every animal. On recordings withheld from training, 75% of detections were seizures and 14 of 22 reference seizures were detected, whereas the source model and a model trained without these animals detected none. NED-Net supports evaluating and adapting detectors to local recordings.

papers.title: BrainCodes: A Lightweight EEG Foundation Model over Discrete Neural Codes
papers.abstract: Recent electroencephalography (EEG) foundation models increasingly emphasize model scale, potentially limiting their deployment on resource-constrained devices and in everyday environments. We argue that transferable EEG features can instead be learned with a compact architecture and introduce BrainCodes, a lightweight foundation model pretrained through self-supervised learning on more than 800 hours of recordings from over 1,000 participants. Our architecture combines a quantization-based neural tokenizer with a spatiotemporal encoder that supports arbitrary electrode configurations. The pretraining objective explicitly encourages representations that capture spatial connectivity through channel positional encoding, and sensitivity to narrowband neural oscillations through an auxiliary training objective. Our model matches or surpasses the state of the art across diverse neurophysiological monitoring tasks, including sleep staging, attention assessment, and cognitive load estimation. BrainCodes transfers effectively to low-resource wearable devices while using up to 97% fewer trainable parameters than comparable architectures. Beyond predictive accuracy, our evaluation framework characterizes the geometry and invariances of learned EEG representations across measurable spatial, temporal, and spectral signal properties.

papers.title: From labels to latents: revealing state-dependent hippocampal computations and non-spatial replay with Jump Latent Variable Model
papers.abstract: Neural activity is often interpreted by imposing external labels (e.g., position during locomotion) and decoding within that space (e.g. replay). While powerful, such supervision can mask structure in the data that do not correspond to the label. Unsupervised methods, in turn, often assume smooth latent dynamics and miss genuine discontinuities. We introduce a conceptually simple, computationally efficient latent variable model that infers both (i) the latent variables organizing population activity and (ii) whether their dynamics are continuous or fragmented in time. Fitting reduces to an expectation-maximization (EM) procedure that alternates two operations familiar to systems neuroscience - tuning-curve estimation and label decoding - without requiring external labels. Applied to rodent hippocampal recordings, our method identifies a continuity-fragmentation axis that characterizes population activity across sleep-wake brain states, modulated by cholinergic inputs. For a spatial navigation task, the model reveals distinct population patterns at the same physical position that supervised spatial decoding fails to detect. Moreover, the model enables replay analysis beyond spatial trajectories, and finds prevalent pre-play events associated with immobile and off-maze behaviors and post-task replay of locomotion. By not relying on externally imposed spatial labels, our approach exposes structure that supervised approaches obscure and provides a powerful tool for datasets lacking behavioral tracking.

Applied to rodent hippocampus, it identifies a cholinergic-modulated continuity-fragmentation axis across sleep-wake states, reveals position-independent population patterns missed by supervised spatial decoding, and uncovers prevalent non-spatial pre-play and post-task locomotor replay.

papers.title: Sleep reactivation shapes memories of event and its temporal structure
papers.abstract: Episodic memory provides a temporal scaffold that organizes past experiences according to their sequential occurrence. While memories are reactivated and consolidated during sleep, it remains unknown how exogenous reactivation reshapes memories of complex events, particularly the temporal structure that binds individual elements across time. In this preregistered study, 35 participants encoded neutral and aversive narratives composed of image sequences, with auditory context shifts defining event boundaries. During post-encoding slow-wave sleep, closed-loop targeted memory reactivation (TMR) delivered boundary-associated auditory cues time-locked to the up-state of slow oscillations. Reactivation led to faster, more confident, and more liberal recognition responses for cued than uncued memories. However, reactivation exerted a time-dependent effect on temporal-order memory, impairing it immediately after sleep but attenuating forgetting one week later. This behavioral dissociation was paralleled at the neural level: stronger cue-elicited theta activity predicted superior recognition of neutral, but not aversive event content, whereas greater theta responses were associated with poorer temporal-order memory for the same events. Together, these findings suggest that sleep reactivation does not uniformly strengthen episodic memories. Rather, it selectively prioritizes access to event content while reorganizing temporal relations among event elements, revealing distinct, time-dependent consequences of sleep reactivation for different components of complex experiences.

papers.title: Associations Between Biomarkers of Alzheimer's Disease and Sleep in Cognitively Unimpaired Older Adults.
papers.abstract: Sleep disturbances have been implicated as a risk factor for developing Alzheimer's disease (AD), but evidence linking plasma AD biomarkers to sleep in cognitively unimpaired individuals remains limited. The present study examined associations between evening, morning, and overnight changes in plasma AD biomarkers and measures of sleep macro- and microstructure and subjective sleep quality in older adults. Forty cognitively unimpaired adults aged 55 to 75 years (20 females) without sleep or mental disorders underwent overnight polysomnography. Plasma AD biomarkers p-tau181, p-tau217, t-tau, Aβ42, Aβ40, and Aβ42/40 were assessed in the evening and in the morning and related to sleep macro- and microstructure (sleep spindles, EEG spectral power), and subjective sleep measures by using correlational analyzes. Higher evening t-tau and p-tau181 were associated with reduced N3 sleep, whereas higher morning t-tau and greater overnight increases in t-tau were related to longer nocturnal wakefulness. Amyloid-β measures showed the most consistent associations with sleep microstructure. Higher Aβ42 and Aβ40 concentrations were associated with shorter duration and lower density of sleep spindles, particularly at frontal sites. Higher evening and morning amyloid-β concentrations were also associated with lower alpha, beta, and spindle-frequency EEG power, mainly during non-rapid eye movement sleep. Tau associations with EEG spectral power were less consistent. In cognitively unimpaired older adults, plasma AD biomarkers were associated with PSG sleep features, especially amyloid-β markers with sleep microstructure. These exploratory, correlational findings suggest that sleep spindles and spectral power may reflect early AD-related biological processes but require replication in larger cohorts.

papers.title: Daytime Napping and Associative-Memory Retrieval Speed: An Exploratory Behavioral and EEG Study
papers.abstract: Purpose: To test whether a daytime nap was associated with improved associative-recognition performance relative to monitored wakefulness and to determine where any response-time (RT) difference occurred in the RT distribution. Methods: Fifteen healthy students completed nap and wake sessions in a within-participant design. Each session included word-pair learning, immediate recognition, a 60-min interval, and delayed recognition without additional study. Trial-level log RT was the focal outcome; accuracy and electroencephalography (EEG) were complementary outcomes. Results: The RT Condition-by-Time interaction was significant (b = -0.063, 95% CI [-0.117, -0.009], p = .027). Responses were 6.7% faster after the nap (p = .010) but did not change after wakefulness (p = .704), with the difference concentrated among slower responses. Accuracy showed no condition-specific change (p = .401). Nap EEG showed aperiodic spectral slowing and stronger periodic sigma activity, but no EEG measure explained the RT effect. Conclusions: Daytime napping was associated with faster delayed associative recognition, primarily through attenuation of the slowest responses. The exploratory findings warrant larger confirmatory studies.

papers.title: Differentiating linked cognitive states under task demand and sleep restriction: toward an experimental framework for operational monitoring.
papers.abstract: Real-world settings involve multiple interacting cognitive states such as mental workload, drowsiness, fatigue, and mind wandering, yet these are typically studied in isolation. A critical question is whether these states can be empirically differentiated given that they share overlapping behavioral and physiological signatures. We investigated whether task difficulty and sleep restriction produce dissociable effects across these states, and whether their response patterns reflect distinct underlying mechanisms or a common cognitive resource using a unified framework. Participants from operational populations (Study 1: n = 40; Study 2: n = 27) performed three complementary tasks (MATB-II, N-Back, and SART) under two manipulations: task difficulty and partial sleep restriction, targeting cognitive load and alertness. Increasing task difficulty degraded performance and increased perceived workload and fatigue across tasks. In contrast, sleep restriction primarily elevated subjective drowsiness and mind wandering, with smaller, task-dependent effects on performance. These findings provide evidence that cognitive and physiological states influencing situational awareness can be differentiated using complementary manipulations and characterized through distinct behavioral and subjective measures. This distinction provides a foundation for future predictive and monitoring approaches in applied settings.

papers.title: Aperiodic neural activity predicts cortical excitability in TMS-EEG
papers.abstract: Background: Fluctuating cortical excitability states are inherent to and critical for brain function. They can be probed non-invasively using transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) combined with electroencephalography (EEG) by measuring early local TMS-evoked potentials (EL-TEPs). Pre-stimulus periodic neural activity can predict fluctuating excitability states. To what extent aperiodic neural activity represents a marker of cortical excitability has not been explored. Objectives: We investigated the relationship between pre-stimulus aperiodic and periodic neural activity and EL-TEP amplitude in both the primary motor cortex (M1) and dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC). Methods: Single-pulse TMS was delivered to the left M1 or left DLPFC in 29 and 11 healthy adults, respectively, while EEG was recorded simultaneously. Pre-stimulus EEG was parameterized into aperiodic and periodic components to extract the aperiodic exponent (slope of 1/f-like activity), alpha power (8-13 Hz), and beta power (13-30 Hz). EL-TEP peak-to-peak amplitudes were extracted from approximately 20-65 ms after the TMS pulse. Results: Aperiodic exponent showed a strong negative relationship with EL-TEP amplitude in both M1 and DLPFC, with steeper 1/f-like slopes associated with smaller EL-TEP amplitudes. Inconsistent relationships were found between alpha and beta power with EL-TEP amplitude across the two regions. Conclusions: These findings indicate that pre-stimulus aperiodic neural activity influences cortical excitability in both motor and prefrontal areas. Notably, the aperiodic exponent exhibited stronger associations with cortical excitability compared to periodic alpha or beta power. Brain-state-dependent protocols may benefit from real-time extraction of aperiodic exponent as a target feature to improve the precision and efficacy of TMS.

papers.title: Portable polysomnography-derived multi-domain EEG markers of anesthetic state transitions during propofol anesthesia for gastrointestinal endoscopy.
papers.abstract: Propofol anesthesia is widely used for gastrointestinal (GI) endoscopy, but electroencephalographic (EEG) features of anesthetic state transitions in this brief and stimulus-rich setting remain incompletely characterized. This study aimed to describe clinically interpretable EEG markers across anesthetic stages using portable polysomnography (PSG)-derived six-channel EEG. In this prospective observational study, 31 adults undergoing GI endoscopy under propofol-based anesthesia underwent continuous portable PSG recording. EEG analyses focused on six scalp channels (F3, F4, C3, C4, O1, and O2) across four clinically defined stages: baseline, induction, maintenance, and recovery. Relative spectral power, spectral edge frequency at 95% cumulative power (SEF95), and spindle-like event metrics were quantified. Sensor-level functional connectivity was assessed using weighted phase-lag index, imaginary coherence, and amplitude envelope correlation (AEC). Spectral and spindle-like event measures were analyzed using linear mixed-effects models, and connectivity differences were assessed using permutation-based paired tests with false discovery rate correction. Relative delta power decreased from baseline and induction to maintenance and recovery, whereas theta, alpha, sigma, and beta relative power and SEF95 generally increased. Spindle-like event density differed across stages and was highest during recovery, while mean duration and peak frequency remained relatively stable within the 11-16 Hz range. Functional connectivity showed metric-specific modulation: AEC demonstrated the most widespread stage-related differences, whereas phase-based connectivity measures showed only limited edge-specific changes after correction for multiple comparisons. Portable PSG-derived six-channel EEG captured stage-related spectral, spindle-like event, and sensor-level connectivity changes during propofol anesthesia for GI endoscopy. These findings identify candidate EEG features for future evaluation of emergence detection and atypical anesthetic-state identification during procedural anesthesia. Their utility for real-time propofol titration or excessive-sedation warning requires prospective validation.

These findings identify candidate EEG markers for anesthetic state transitions.

papers.title: The role of histamine in narcolepsy type 1: a narrative review.
papers.abstract: Narcolepsy type 1 (NT1) is a chronic neurological disorder characterized mainly by impaired wakefulness maintenance and dysregulated rapid eye movement (REM) sleep, which markedly affects patients' daytime functioning and quality of life. The core pathological basis of NT1 is the selective loss of orexinergic neurons. The orexinergic system regulates histaminergic neurons in the tuberomammillary nucleus (TMN) through anatomical projections and functional excitation, while the histaminergic system contributes to cortical activation, arousal maintenance, and attention regulation. Therefore, the orexinergic and histaminergic systems can be regarded as interconnected and functionally complementary components of the arousal network. Previous studies have suggested alterations in histaminergic signaling in NT1, although the specific mechanisms underlying its role in NT1 remain incompletely understood. Current evidence suggests that histamine may play a modulatory role in NT1-associated phenotypes. This review summarizes the physiological functions of the histaminergic system in arousal regulation and discusses its interaction with the orexinergic system. It further analyzes the role of HA in NT1, its influence on clinical phenotypes, and related therapeutic strategies, with the aim of providing insights for mechanistic research and precision treatment of NT1.

papers.title: Peripheral GRM2 and GRM3 mRNA Alterations and Clinical Correlates in Insomnia Disorder: A Case-Control Pilot Study.
papers.abstract: This pilot study examined whether peripheral GRM2/GRM3 mRNA expression differed between chronic insomnia disorder (ID) and healthy controls (HCs) and correlated with emotional and polysomnographic (PSG) features. After PSG screening, 43 patients with chronic ID meeting DSM-5-TR criteria and 34 HCs with comparable age and sex distributions were included. Mood, sleep, and PSG parameters were assessed, and peripheral GRM2/GRM3 mRNA was quantified by RT-qPCR. Statistical analyses comprised group comparisons, age- and sex-adjusted regression, partial correlations with false discovery rate (FDR) correction, Bayesian analyses, sensitivity analyses, and exploratory receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analyses. Compared with HCs, ID patients showed greater depressive and anxiety symptoms, poorer subjective sleep quality, and altered sleep architecture. Peripheral GRM2 and GRM3 mRNA expression was lower in ID patients, with both differences remaining significant after adjustment for age and sex (P=0.001; P=0.029). The apparent area under the curves (AUCs) were 0.744, 0.666, and 0.769 for GRM2, GRM3, and the combined model, respectively; corresponding cross-validated mean AUCs were 0.745, 0.645, and 0.732. Both GRM2 and GRM3 showed associations with emotional and sleep measures; the GRM3-PHQ-9 association remained significant after FDR correction (r=-0.373, P adj=0.020), while the GRM2-REM association showed Bayesian support (BF=4.473). These associations were attenuated after further adjustment for diagnostic group. Lower peripheral GRM2 and GRM3 expression was associated with chronic ID, with exploratory associations with selected emotional and sleep measures. These findings identify peripheral GRM2/GRM3 as candidate molecular correlates of ID. Independent external validation is required before clinical diagnostic application.

papers.title: The influence of circadian variables on ecotoxicology metabolomics.
papers.abstract: Ecotoxicologists are using metabolomics increasingly to gain insight into toxicological mechanisms and sublethal effects of chemical exposures. Metabolomics offers a sensitive multi-parameter approach that can detect biochemical responses not obvious using apical and behavioural endpoints. This includes the responses to very low-dose toxicant exposures, variations in the physico-chemical state of experimental media, and even the progression of circadian rhythms. Consequently, repeatability and comparability of metabolomics experiments relies on the control and reporting of these features. In this systematic quantitative literature review, we examine recent ecotoxicology research to determine the rate and quality of reporting of circadian timing and other variables that influence circadian rhythms and the associated metabolome. We found that most circadian variables are underreported and call for further research into the influence of their manipulation on the metabolome.

papers.title: Acute creatine-guanidinoacetate supplementation improves regional brain oxygenation following sleep deprivation: A randomized controlled trial.
papers.abstract: Background: Sleep deprivation impairs cognitive performance and may alter regional cerebral oxygenation. Nutritional strategies that preserve brain oxygenation could help mitigate these adverse effects. Aim: To compare the acute effects of creatine-guanidinoacetate (GAA), molecular hydrogen inhalation, caffeine, and placebo on regional brain oxygenation and attention-related performance following sleep deprivation.Methods: Twenty-two healthy young adults completed a 24-hour sleep deprivation protocol and were randomly assigned to receive creatine-GAA, molecular hydrogen inhalation, caffeine, or placebo. Brain oxygenation was assessed using functional near-infrared spectroscopy over the frontal, temporal, and occipital cortices during a modified attention network test. Alertness, executive control, orienting, reaction time, and accuracy were also evaluated.Summary: Creatine-GAA significantly increased frontal oxygen saturation (50.8% ± 4.1% to 61.0% ± 5.9%, P = 0.01; Cohen's d = 2.00) and temporal oxygen saturation (63.1% ± 4.8% to 70.2% ± 2.6%, P = 0.01; Cohen's d = 1.83). Significant time-by-treatment interactions were observed for frontal oxygen saturation (P = 0.043; ηp2 = 0.331), temporal oxygen saturation (P = 0.021; ηp2 = 0.428), and occipital total hemoglobin (P = 0.022; ηp2 = 0.405). No significant between-group differences were observed in attention-related outcomes. Acute creatine-GAA supplementation improved regional brain oxygenation following sleep deprivation, particularly in the frontal and temporal cortices, without measurable improvements in attention-related performance. These preliminary findings support further investigation of creatine-based nutritional strategies in larger randomized controlled trials.

papers.title: Sleep, inflammation, and pain in musculoskeletal rehabilitation: a structured integrative review of neurobiological mechanisms and non-pharmacological pain management strategies.
papers.abstract: Sleep disturbance, inflammation, and persistent pain may reinforce one another, compromising musculoskeletal rehabilitation. To synthesize evidence on mechanisms linking sleep, inflammation, and pain and identify relevant non-pharmacological interventions. This structured integrative review examined peer-reviewed studies published from January 2010 to December 2025, identified through PubMed, Scopus, PEDro, and SciELO. Reporting and synthesis were guided by SANRA and EQUATOR recommendations. Fifty-seven studies were included: 24 experimental or observational studies, 17 systematic reviews or meta-analyses, and 16 narrative or integrative reviews. Sleep restriction was associated with changes in interleukin-6, tumor necrosis factor-α, and C-reactive protein, with responses varying across populations and protocols. Prostaglandins and bradykinin may promote nociceptive sensitization, while disrupted sleep may impair descending pain inhibition. Exercise, manual therapy, neuromuscular electrical stimulation, low-level laser therapy, and sleep-focused behavioral interventions showed mechanistic plausibility, although confirmatory trials remain limited. Sleep assessment and sleep-focused interventions should be considered within multimodal musculoskeletal pain management, while further controlled research clarifies clinical effectiveness.

It concluded that exercise, manual therapy, electrical stimulation, laser therapy, and sleep-focused behavioral interventions have mechanistic plausibility but limited confirmatory trial evidence.

papers.title: A 6-8-Hour Nighttime Sleep Strategy and Subsequent Cognitive Performance: A Target Trial Emulation Study.
papers.abstract: Sleep duration is a modifiable factor linked to cognitive aging among middle-aged and older adults, but existing evidence is largely correlational. Using observational data in which sleep duration was self-reported, we emulated a target trial to estimate the effect of maintaining a 6-8 h nighttime sleep strategy on subsequent cognitive performance. This target trial emulation study analyzed participants from the China Health and Retirement Longitudinal Study (CHARLS), a longitudinal, nationally representative prospective cohort of Chinese adults aged 45 years and older, and followed them from 2011 to 2020. Nocturnal sleep duration was self-reported at every wave. The 6-8 h sleep strategy was compared with a non-6-8 h strategy (<6h or >8h) using intention-to-treat (ITT), per-protocol (PP), and inverse probability of censoring weighting (IPCW)-weighted PP analyses. Primary outcome was the total cognitive score (range 0-21) after 9 years. Groups were balanced by 1:1 propensity-score matching (PSM) on 18 baseline covariates, and missing baseline covariate data were handled by multiple imputation by chained equations. Of 8147 eligible participants, 2341 matched pairs were included after PSM. The 6-8 h sleep strategy was consistently associated with higher cognitive scores than the non-6-8 h strategy in the ITT analysis (β = 0.237, 95% CI 0.016 to 0.458, p=0.036), the unweighted PP analysis (β = 0.394, 95% CI -0.013 to 0.801, p=0.058), and the IPCW-weighted PP analysis (β = 0.614, 95% CI 0.176 to 1.052, p=0.006). All estimates were modest in absolute terms, corresponding to 5.3% and 13.7% of one standard deviation of the outcome for the ITT and weighted PP analyses. The dose-response curve showed a nonlinear, inverted U-shaped association (P for non-linearity <0.001), with the highest predicted cognition at about 6.7 h of sleep. Neither sex nor age modified the association (P for interaction 0.84 and 0.27). By emulating a target trial with repeated prospective cohort data, this study moves beyond simple association and suggests that maintaining 6-8 h of self-reported nighttime sleep is associated with modestly higher subsequent cognitive performance. Target trial emulation improves the rigour of effect estimation but does not eliminate residual confounding, exposure misclassification or selective attrition; the findings require confirmation in studies using objective sleep assessment and more complete control of time-varying confounding.

papers.title: A brain-behavior generative model links individual brain dynamics to perceptual decisions
papers.abstract: Perceptual decision speed varies across individuals and trials. Explaining this variability requires linking individual brain anatomy, neural dynamics, and behavior, yet whole-brain models typically reproduce brain signals without behavior, whereas behavioral models lack anatomical constraints. Here we introduce a brain-behavior generative model in which whole-brain dynamics on each participant's structural connectome generate both single-trial electroencephalography (EEG) and reaction times. Fitted to 17 participants performing motion discrimination, the models reproduced individual event-related potentials and reaction-time distributions. Joint fitting enabled the models to predict whether held-out trials were relatively fast or slow within each stimulus condition. In silico silencing further predicted where, how, and when each person's brain controls decision speed. Sensorimotor regions affected decision speed consistently across most participants, whereas the same parietal region had opposite effects in different participants. These opposite effects reflected whether the region acted mainly through network dynamics or the decision readout. Temporal analyses suggested that early activity largely set decision speed, whereas late EEG mainly tracked the unfolding decision. These results show that brain-behavior generative modeling can link individual brain dynamics to perceptual decisions and yield testable predictions of why decision speed varies across individuals and trials.

papers.title: Subject-independent classification of ADHD from pediatric EEG: a leakage-aware deep learning framework with interpretable neurophysiological mapping.
papers.abstract: The use of electroencephalography (EEG) in automated screening of Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) has created a large body of literature that suggests promising outcomes, with reported classification accuracies often above 90%. A major methodological issue suggests that a substantial part of these results are actually due to data leakage, whereby EEG epochs pertaining to the same subject end up in both training and testing sets, allowing classifiers to capitalize on features specific to the individual rather than on genuine disorder-related biomarkers. We assessed the performance of three classical machine learning algorithms, namely, Logistic Regression (LR), Random Forest (RF), and Support Vector Machine (SVM), as well as three deep learning models: Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM), Convolutional Neural Network (CNN), and CNN-BiLSTM, on a standard pediatric EEG dataset containing 121 children and 4,173 epochs. The performance of each model was compared in terms of both segment-wise cross-validation (Protocol A) and subject-wise cross-validation (without any data leakage, Protocol B).To evaluate neurotopographic plausibility without making unsupported causal assertions, we applied Deep SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) to the best-generalizing architecture. The performance discrepancy was substantial. Under segment-wise evaluation, the SVM operating on power spectral density (PSD) features reached 90.0% accuracy (95% CI: [89.1%, 90.9%], AUC = 0.96). However, the same model dropped to 65.6% (95% CI: [62.1%, 69.1%], AUC = 0.72) under subject-wise evaluation-a statistically significant 24.4 percentage point collapse (p < 0.001, Wilcoxon signed-rank). In contrast, deep architectures learning directly from raw EEG were resilient: the stand-alone CNN lost only 2.5 percentage points, achieving 72.7% accuracy (95% CI: [66.0%, 79.4%], AUC = 0.72, recall = 88.0%) on completely unseen participants. Post-hoc SHAP attribution identified the highest relative contributions in frontal (F3, Fz, F4) and central (Cz) electrodes, aligning with established ADHD neurophysiology. Hand-engineered spectral features are highly vulnerable to identity leakage, whereas end-to-end convolutional models generalize across subjects with realistic, uninflated performance. Strict subject-wise validation is strongly recommended as standard practice for translational EEG research.

papers.title: Sleep in Different Types of Dizziness.
papers.abstract: Sleep disturbances and dizziness are frequently comorbid, yet the specific sleep profiles across different vestibular disorders remain poorly characterized. This study aimed to investigate distinct sleep signatures in patients with benign paroxysmal positional vertigo (BPPV), vestibular migraine (VM), and persistent postural-perceptual dizziness (PPPD) compared to healthy controls. We conducted a cross-sectional study with 90 participants: 24 healthy controls, 21 with BPPV, 23 with PPPD, and 22 with VM. Sleep was assessed using a multimodal approach: 14-day actigraphy, a single-night home sleep apnea test (Watch-PAT), and validated questionnaires, including the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI), Dizziness Handicap Inventory (DHI), and Beck Anxiety/Depression Inventories. All dizziness groups reported significantly worse subjective sleep quality and higher psychological burden than controls. However, each disorder presented a unique objective signature: BPPV: Characterized by objective sleep fragmentation and a markedly higher Apnea-Hypopnea Index (AHI: 31.5) and Oxygen Desaturation Index (ODI: 16). These patients also showed increased nocturnal restlessness (L5). PPPD: Demonstrated a "sleep paradox" with the highest objective sleep efficiency but the poorest subjective perception (PSQI: 11.0). Patients showed reduced daytime activity (M10) and rigid sleep routines with virtually no weekend-weekday get-up time difference. VM: Distinguished by the shortest total sleep time and pronounced, though not statistically significant, "social jetlag", reflected by a 120-min discrepancy between weekend and weekday get-up times. Dizziness is not a homogeneous entity regarding sleep. The distinct signatures found suggest that clinical management should be tailored: screening for sleep apnea in BPPV, addressing the objective-subjective disconnect in PPPD via cognitive-behavioral approaches, and managing sleep deprivation and circadian regularity in VM.

papers.title: Multi-Metric EEG Connectivity and Graph Analysis Reveal Altered Resting-State Networks in Major Depressive Disorder.
papers.abstract: EEG functional-connectivity studies in major depressive disorder (MDD) have produced inconsistent findings, partly because different estimators capture distinct aspects of neural coupling. We implemented a multi-metric resting-state EEG approach combining linear, phase-based, nonlinear, and graph-theoretical measures to characterize frequency-dependent sensor-level connectivity alterations and identify sensor-level network patterns relevant to depression-related dysconnectivity. Resting-state EEG from 30 DSM-IV MDD participants and 28 healthy controls was analyzed using a 19-channel 10-20 montage. After MNE-Python preprocessing, including filtering, ICA-based artifact removal, current source density (CSD) transformation, and symmetric orthogonalization, coherence, PLV, PLI, and MI were computed across theta, alpha, and beta bands. Edge-wise differences were tested using Brunner-Munzel with Holm correction, confirmed with Westfall-Young maxT correction, and summarized using Hedges' g and graph measures. MDD showed frequency- and metric-dependent sensor-level connectivity alterations. Theta coherence, PLV, and PLI were dominated by lower connectivity across frontal-to-posterior, fronto-central, temporal/posterior-temporal, parieto-occipital, and central-to-occipital sensor pairs, whereas theta MI showed few increased frontal/fronto-temporal effects. Alpha findings were more selective, with mainly lower coherence and PLV across frontopolar/frontal-to-central, fronto-midline, and posterior links, while alpha MI showed a limited mixed pattern. In beta, coherence, PLV, and PLI showed sparse robust reductions, whereas beta MI showed widespread increased statistical dependence. Graph-theoretical summaries at 20% proportional density showed mainly lower mean weighted strength and global efficiency in theta- and alpha-band networks. These findings indicate frequency- and metric-dependent resting-state EEG sensor-level connectivity alterations in MDD. The dominant pattern was lower theta/alpha connectivity across distributed sensor pairs, alongside increased beta MI-based dependence. The results provide corrected, effect-size-informed evidence of altered inter-sensor coordination without establishing dysfunction of specific cortical regions or named networks. This framework may support future hypothesis-driven research in independent, clinically annotated, higher-density EEG or multimodal datasets.

papers.title: MSANet: a multi-scale spatiotemporal adaptive network for EEG-based driver fatigue recognition.
papers.abstract: Electroencephalography (EEG)-based driver fatigue recognition remains challenging because fatigue-related patterns are distributed across multiple temporal scales, inter-channel relationships vary across samples, and inter-individual differences complicate cross-subject transfer. To address these issues, a multi-scale spatiotemporal adaptive network (MSANet) is proposed for EEG-based driver fatigue recognition. The framework introduces a multi-granularity patch temporal gate (MGPTG) to model locally continuous temporal contexts, stable graph node enhancement (SGNE) to enhance channel-node features before dynamic graph construction, and an adaptive classifier gate (ACG) to combine cosine-based and affine decision geometries. MSANet was evaluated on two public simulated-driving EEG datasets using a cross-subject transfer protocol, in which the target-subject samples were stratified with a partition ratio of 0.5 into a labeled adaptation subset and a held-out test subset. MSANet achieved an accuracy (ACC) of 83.64% and an F1-score (F1) of 83.74% on Dataset I, and 74.64% ACC and 72.92% F1 on Dataset II. The results indicate strong numerical performance on Dataset I and competitive performance on Dataset II. Subject-level statistical analysis was additionally conducted to distinguish mean performance differences from differences that are consistently supported across subjects. Ablation results showed lower mean performance after removing MGPTG, SGNE, or ACG under the evaluated settings. These findings support further evaluation of the proposed stage-specific temporal, graph-node, and classification mechanisms for cross-subject transfer in EEG-based driver fatigue recognition.

papers.title: Learning Out of Hours: A Narrative Review of Balancing Responsibility, Supervision, and Fatigue in Junior Doctor Training.
papers.abstract: Out-of-hours work is an integral component of postgraduate medical training and exposes junior doctors to clinical responsibility, uncertainty, competing demands, and acute deterioration in circumstances that may differ substantially from routine daytime practice. These conditions can provide valuable opportunities for experiential learning, but they can also reduce educational value when responsibility is accompanied by inadequate supervision, excessive workload or fatigue. This narrative review examines out-of-hours work as a learning environment for junior doctors, integrating literature on workplace learning, autonomy and supervision, prioritisation and decision-making, deterioration and escalation, handover and teamwork, sleep disruption and fatigue, and educational interventions designed to prepare trainees for out-of-hours practice. The literature suggests that the educational value of out-of-hours work arises not from independence alone, but from meaningful clinical responsibility within an appropriately supported environment. Responsibility can provide opportunities for autonomous initial assessment, prioritisation, and decision-making under uncertainty, while the recognition of personal limits and appropriate escalation are themselves components of developing clinical judgement. Simulation and structured preparation may help trainees rehearse these demands before substantial clinical responsibility is assumed, while feedback, reflection, and review of subsequent patient outcomes can help convert clinical exposure into learning. However, excessive workload, inadequate supervision, and fatigue may impair both the opportunity and the capacity to learn. Out-of-hours training should therefore aim to preserve authentic responsibility while ensuring that autonomy is graded to capability, senior support remains accessible, workload is manageable, and opportunities for feedback and recovery are maintained. We propose that effective out-of-hours learning occurs within a zone of meaningful responsibility in which trainees are sufficiently challenged to develop clinical judgement without becoming unsupported or physiologically unsustainable. Designing this environment requires attention not only to individual preparedness but also to supervision, staffing, workload, handover, feedback, and rota design.

papers.title: Entrainment of the Arabidopsis circadian clock to skeleton photoperiods
papers.abstract: Entrainment aligns the phase of the circadian clock and its outputs with 24 h fluctuations in the environmental conditions. One approach for investigating entrainment involves the application of skeleton photoperiods. In these protocols, light pulses are used to demarcate dawn and dusk, with the organism otherwise remaining under constant darkness. Historically, the consequences of skeleton photoperiod entrainment have been investigated by tracking behavioural responses in mammalian and insect models. In comparison, effects of skeleton photoperiod entrainment upon the plant circadian oscillator have received less attention. Using promoter-luciferase reporters for the Arabidopsis thaliana circadian clock, we monitored clock function during both entrainment to skeleton photoperiods, and subsequent free-running conditions. This enabled us to access molecular responses of the plant circadian oscillator to skeleton light conditions. We identified that individual circadian oscillator components in Arabidopsis can entrain to skeleton photoperiods. When these skeleton photoperiods were extended to represent long-day conditions, the oscillator underwent a phase jump relative to intact photoperiod entrainment such that it interpreted the dusk light pulse as dawn, and vice versa. This mirrors phase jumps that have been reported for rodent and insect behaviour following entrainment to long skeleton photoperiods, supporting the idea that phase jumps under skeleton photoperiod entrainment are a universal feature of circadian entrainment. Our results provide important context for the interpretation of physiological and developmental phenotypes of plants under modified light conditions.

papers.title: Artificial intelligence applications in intracranial electroencephalography for epilepsy management: Insights from AI in Epilepsy 2025.
papers.abstract: Intracranial electroencephalography (iEEG) provides direct recordings of cortical activity and remains central to the presurgical evaluation of drug-resistant focal epilepsy. However, the high dimensionality and complexity of iEEG data increasingly challenge conventional visual interpretation. Artificial intelligence (AI) methods have accelerated quantitative analyses in electrophysiology, supporting localization, outcome prediction, and therapeutic decision-making in epilepsy. This article reviews recent advances in the application of AI to iEEG in epilepsy and in particular stereo-EEG, although the concepts discussed are broadly relevant across iEEG modalities. Although many of these approaches have shown encouraging results, the current evidence remains largely preliminary, with most studies being retrospective, single-center investigations that lack independent external validation. AI-based integration of iEEG with multimodal magnetic resonance imaging shows promise for improving surgical planning in drug-resistant focal epilepsy. Concurrently, early studies suggest that AI-driven iEEG analysis may enhance epileptogenic zone identification by detecting subtle electrophysiological signatures, network interactions, and temporal dynamics. These multimodal frameworks emphasize distributed epileptic networks rather than isolated focal abnormalities. AI is also reshaping how iEEG-guided stimulation is designed and interpreted. Data-driven approaches have the potential to optimize stimulation parameters, predict network responses, and clarify mechanisms underlying diagnostic and therapeutic stimulation, laying the groundwork for adaptive, patient-specific neuromodulation. Beyond short-term epilepsy monitoring, AI applications increasingly incorporate continuous sensing, longitudinal network modeling, and integration with implantable neurotechnology platforms. Although these developments require prospective multicenter studies with external validation before widespread clinical implementation, advances in multimodal data integration, interpretable modeling, and continuous sensing position AI-enhanced iEEG as an emerging platform for precision brain network medicine for epilepsy.

papers.title: Altitude-induced plasticity of respiratory central-peripheral chemoreflex interaction.
papers.abstract: Stable breathing depends on the integrated action of central and peripheral chemoreceptors, but the nature of this interaction in humans and its physiological importance remain controversial. Previous studies reported additive, hypo-additive and hyper-additive responses across species, preparations and protocols. Here, we used a novel method to quantify peripheral chemoreflex sensitivity across graded levels of central chemoreceptor activation to test whether central-peripheral chemoreceptor interaction in awake humans is fixed or state dependent. At low altitude, the form of interaction varied across individuals, with most showing additive responses (12/17) and a substantial subset showing hypo-additivity (5/17). After 7-10 days of acclimatization to 3500 m, all five hypo-additive individuals became additive, and four additive participants became hyper-additive. This shift in interaction towards hyper-additivity provides the first evidence that central-peripheral chemoreceptor integration is plastic. Plasticity during wakefulness was not associated with individual differences in central sleep apnoea severity at high altitude. Thus, our findings confirm that central-peripheral chemoreceptor interaction differs among individuals and suggest that the form of interaction can be reshaped by hypobaric hypoxic stress. KEY POINTS: How central and peripheral chemoreceptor drives to breathe interact in humans and whether this process is plastic remains uncertain. We quantified peripheral chemoreflex sensitivity to hypoxia (PChS) across graded levels of central chemoreceptor activation at low altitude and after 7-10 days of high-altitude exposure (3500 m). Seventeen participants performed repeated modified rebreathing tests with end-tidal P O 2 fixed at 150 (hyperoxia), 60 and 45 mmHg (hypoxia). PChS was computed at 1 mmHg intervals of end-tidal P C O 2 ( P ETC O 2 ) from linear regression of the difference in ventilation between hypoxic and hyperoxic conditions vs. calculated arterial oxygen saturation (ScO2) (L·min-1·mmHg-1·%ScO2 -1). At low altitude, PChS increased with P ETC O 2 in all individuals; the relationship was linear (no interaction) in 12 participants, and 5 showed hypo-additivity. After acclimatization, central and peripheral chemoreflex sensitivities increased. All hypo-additive individuals became additive; four additive individuals became hyper-additive. Central-peripheral chemoreceptor interaction is plastic in humans and can shift towards hyper-additivity with sustained hypobaric hypoxia.

papers.title: N-back electroencephalography asymmetry and peripheral immune cell subpopulation composition.
papers.abstract: Cognitive deficits such as working memory impairment and peripheral inflammation frequently occur together in neuropsychiatric conditions, yet the relationship between them remains poorly understood. To address this gap, the present study examines these associations in healthy young adults to establish baseline relationships between peripheral immune cell subpopulations and neural activity without clinical confounds. The aim of this study is to investigate whether the relative proportions of peripheral immune cell subpopulations are associated with EEG asymmetry during a working memory task and with task performance. EEG data were recorded from 24 healthy participants during a 2-back working memory task. Relative EEG asymmetry indices were computed for four frequency bands: alpha, beta, delta, and theta. 2-back task performance was also calculated. Peripheral blood was collected for DNA extraction and genome-wide DNA methylation analysis to estimate the relative proportions of immune cell subpopulations. Estimated proportions were Center Log-Ratio-transformed. Spearman's correlation and multiple linear regression were used to identify associations between EEG asymmetry, relative immune markers, and n-back task performance. Our analysis revealed that theta asymmetry was associated with CLR-transformed proportions of natural killer cells (p=0.035) and CD4+ T cells (p = 0.027). 2-back task target accuracy was nearly correlated with granulocytes (p = 0.082) and CD8+ T cell proportions (p=0.016); however, these associations did not remain significant after Bonferroni correction. Despite this, both immune markers significantly predicted 2-back target accuracy across three multiple linear regression models (model 1: p = 0.005, model 2: p = 0.002, model 3: p = 0.002).

papers.title: Drosophila Appl loss disrupts proteins in mitochondrial oxidative and glycosylation pathways conserved in Alzheimer's disease.
papers.abstract: The physiological functions of the amyloid precursor protein (APP) remain unclear due to genetic redundancy and complex phenotypes. For decades, Drosophila amyloid precursor protein-like (Appl) research has relied on Appl d, a presumed null allele generated by irradiation. Here, we show that Appl d contains complex chromosomal rearrangements and background mutations confounding the interpretation of gene function. To address this, we created a precise CRISPR toolkit, including a clean null and a reporter allele. Deep proteomic profiling reveals that true Appl loss affects proteins associated with N-linked glycosylation, mitochondrial, and metabolic functions in a distinct signature from the background of Appl d. This conserved metabolic signature mirrors alterations in human patients and mouse Alzheimer's models and is associated with disrupted sleep and locomotion in flies. Our findings correct the genetic understanding of Appl, establishing it as a conserved regulator of metabolic balance essential for neuronal function.

papers.title: Integrating task-state electroencephalography and motor function for intelligent assessment of recovery status from prolonged disorders of consciousness.
papers.abstract: Accurately assessing recovery in patients with prolonged disorders of consciousness (PDoC) is essential for evaluating the therapeutic efficacy and optimizing clinical care. However, substantial individual variability and poorly understood recovery mechanisms render this task exceptionally challenging. We collected task-state electroencephalography and clinical records from 78 PDoC patients to develop an intelligent assessment framework. Power spectral densities (PSDs) and coherence values (CVs) derived from event-related potentials (ERPs) were extracted and integrated with motor function scores to construct a multidimensional feature set. Linear support vector machine (SVM) and logistic regression (LR) models were built and rigorously evaluated via leave-one-out cross-validation (LOOCV). SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) was utilized for visual explanation. The LOOCV indicated that both LR and SVM achieved optimal, similar performance in integrating alpha-band features with motor function (Macro-Average F1-score [Ma-F]: 76.79% versus 75.54%). The Receiver Operating Characteristic curves (with Area Under the Curve values of 77.57% for LR and 72.82% for SVM) and Precision-Recall curves (with Average Precision values of 68.87% for LR and 59.85% for SVM) suggested that the framework performs stably. The reliability curves indicated that both models demonstrate good calibration and are reliable for assessment. The study provides preliminary evidence that alpha-band PSDs and CVs derived from ERPs potentially enhance the motor function assessment performance. This integrated paradigm provides a valuable indicator. Overall, our findings suggest that combining neuroscience with intelligent technology holds promise for improving personalized diagnosis and optimizing the PDoC management.

papers.title: EEG-defined differences in functional networks following beta-band transcranial alternating current stimulation in patients with disorders of consciousness: a pilot study.
papers.abstract: Severe disruption of cortico-thalamocortical circuits underlies disorders of consciousness (DOC). Beta-band (20 Hz) transcranial alternating current stimulation (tACS) can be used to probe frontal oscillatory synchrony, yet its potential to acutely modulate large-scale network dynamics in DOC is unknown. We applied 20 Hz tACS (1 mA) for 30 min over the frontal cortex (F3 and F4, International 10-20 system) in 28 patients with DOC. Offline functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) was used to quantify hemoglobin (HbO)-based functional connectivity (FC) and graph-theoretical network properties, including small-world properties (clustering coefficient, Cp; path length, Lp) and global efficiency (global efficiency, Eg; local efficiency, Eloc) at pre-stimulation resting-state measurement for 5 min (pre-stim), the first post-stimulation resting-state measurement for 5 min (post-stim1), and the second post-stimulation resting-state measurement for 5 min (post-stim2). Subgroups were defined by baseline video-electroencephalography (vEEG) pathology as moderately abnormal (n = 11) and diffuse slowing (n = 14); 3 patients excluded (incomplete vEEG). Frontal 20 Hz tACS was associated with transient enhancement of FC across the measured cortical network at post-stim1 (pFDR < 0.05), selectively strengthening intra-and interhemispheric and intra-nodal connectivity before resolving by post-stim2. Crucially, the effects were pathology-dependent, and visual-motor integration pathways (right occipital lobe to left motor cortex; right primary somatosensory cortex to left occipital lobe) emerged exclusively in DOC patients with moderately abnormal background but not in those with diffuse slowing. Concurrent acute network reorganization at post-stim1 (all p < 0.05) featured increased Cp, Eg, and Eloc, along with decreased Lp, all normalizing by post-stim2. Clinically, Coma Recovery Scale-Revised scores correlated positively with average FC of HbO (pre-stim: r = 0.47; post-stim2: r = 0.41) and Area Under the Curve (AUC) of Eg (pre-stim: r = 0.44), and negatively with AUC of Lp (pre-stim: r = - 0.41; all p < 0.05). Frontal beta-tACS was associated with state-dependent changes in functional network organization in DOC, with dynamic fNIRS measures that may be useful for tracking these changes. These findings provide preliminary descriptive evidence of short-term network changes associated with beta-tACS and may help guide future controlled studies of targeted neuromodulation in patients with DOC.

papers.title: EEG microstate alterations in psychotic depression: prolonged microstate C duration and associations with psychotic symptoms.
papers.abstract: Major Depressive Disorder with psychotic features (MDD-Psy) represents a severe clinical subtype with distinct psychopathology, yet its underlying large-scale brain network dynamics, as measured by resting-state EEG microstates, remain poorly characterized. We compared 68 patients with MDD-Psy and 63 patients with MDD without psychotic features (MDD-NonPsy). Clinical assessment included the Kangduo Antidepressant Scale (KDAS) and the Brief Psychiatric Rating Scale (BPRS). Resting-state EEG microstate parameters (duration, time coverage, occurrence, and transition probabilities) were analyzed. Group comparisons employed Mann-Whitney U/t-tests with False Discovery Rate (FDR) correction. Correlations between microstate alterations and psychotic symptom severity were assessed using Spearman's rank correlation with FDR correction. The groups were comparable in age and sex. The MDD-Psy group exhibited significantly greater severity in thought disturbance, activation, and hostility (all p < 0.001). EEG microstate analysis revealed a significantly prolonged median duration of microstate C, putatively associated with salience-network-related activity in MDD-Psy (91.99 ms) versus MDD-NonPsy (85.56 ms; p-corr = 0.004). Altered transition probabilities characterized MDD-Psy, including increased B→A but decreased B→C and C→A transitions (all p-corr < 0.05). Furthermore, in the combined sample, the duration of microstate C positively correlated with thought disturbance (ρ = 0.243, p-FDR = 0.030), while the reduced B→C transition probability was strongly negatively correlated with both thought disturbance (ρ=-0.393, p-FDR < 0.001) and hostility. Within patients with major depressive disorder, the psychotic subtype is associated with a distinct pattern of aberrant resting-state brain network dynamics relative to the non-psychotic subtype, characterized by prolonged microstate C duration, commonly linked to salience network dynamics and reconfigured temporal transitions between the salience, visual, and auditory networks. The altered visual-to-salience network transition (B → C) demonstrated the most robust association with core psychotic symptom dimensions, including thought disturbance and hostility. These findings suggest that dysregulated dynamic coupling between perceptual processing and salience evaluation may represent a candidate neurophysiological indicator of psychotic features in depression. However, these results should be considered hypothesis-generating preliminary: the high rate of antipsychotic medication use in the MDD-Psy group, the absence of a healthy control group, and the cross-sectional design preclude tentative causal or specificity claims. Future longitudinal studies incorporating medication-naïve patients, healthy controls, and complementary neurophysiological markers are required to validate the clinical utility of these microstate alterations. papers.title: Progress in research on the bidirectional relationship between circadian rhythm and depression: A bibliometric analysis.
papers.abstract: This study used VOSviewer and CiteSpace to conduct a bibliometric analysis of 444 publications on the relationship between circadian rhythms and depression, retrieved from the Web of Science Core Collection (January 2015 to April 2025). Publication numbers remained low until 2017 but increased markedly after 2018, with the United States contributing the largest share. Ian B. Hickie and Joanne S. Carpenter were the most prolific authors; the University of Pittsburgh and Chronobiology International were the most productive institution and journal, respectively. McClung, Dubocovich, and Logan were the top co-cited authors, while frequent keywords included "expression," "sleep," "circadian rhythms," and "melatonin." These findings underscore the growing importance of circadian rhythms in depression pathophysiology and therapy, with future research likely to focus on diagnosis, biomarker identification, individualized treatment, prognosis, and health management.

papers.title: NeuroCodec: EEG-Guided Latent-Domain Generative Model for High-Fidelity Target Speaker Extraction
papers.abstract: Driven by recent advancements in hearing assistive devices, target speaker extraction (TSE) in multi-talker environments has drawn significant attention. To address this, hearing technologies identify attention using neural signals recorded via electroencephalography (EEG) to guide TSE, enabling neuro-steered auditory attention decoding. However, most existing techniques rely on time-frequency masking, which suffers from low fidelity in spectro-temporally overlapping regions and is often restricted to narrowband audio. In contrast, we introduce NeuroCodec, which, to the best of our knowledge, is the first generative EEG-guided TSE framework operating in the latent space of a neural audio codec. Specifically, NeuroCodec models spatial EEG dependencies via graph convolutions and fuses cross-modal EEG and speech representations through attention mechanisms and Mamba-based temporal modeling. We further introduce a six-phase training curriculum that progressively incorporates latent reconstruction, multi-scale spectral, and adversarial objectives to ensure stable, high-fidelity speech generation. Experiments on the public Cocktail Party and KUL datasets show NeuroCodec outperforms baselines, across several perceptual metrics. A listening experiment with 20 participants validated that NeuroCodec offers greater perceptual accuracy, achieving a mean score of 82.24 compared with 49.63 for M3ANet. Additionally, the proposed method is seen to enable 44.1 kHz reconstruction with spectral content extending up to 20 kHz, further supporting the perceptual results. Finally, we extend NeuroCodec with a causal streaming formulation suited for real-time processing, providing a basis for hearing assistive devices.

papers.title: Relative Brain Perfusion Differences and Cognitive Improvement During Multimodal Management in a Patient With Progressive Cognitive Symptoms: A Case Report.
papers.abstract: Progressive cognitive symptoms in older adults may reflect multiple interacting neurologic, vascular, sleep-related, medical, and lifestyle factors, making both etiologic attribution and assessment of treatment response challenging. We report the case of a 72-year-old man with approximately five years of progressive cognitive symptoms, including short-term memory impairment, slowed processing, distractibility, reduced initiative, and executive difficulties, in the setting of a remote cardiac arrest, cardiovascular and cerebrovascular risk, subsequent head trauma, and suspected sleep-disordered breathing. Baseline evaluation included a Self-Administered Gerocognitive Examination (SAGE) score of 9/22, minimal depressive symptoms, continuous performance testing, and adjunctive resting and concentration brain perfusion single-photon emission computed tomography (SPECT). The SPECT findings were interpreted qualitatively as differences in relative regional tracer distribution and were not considered independently diagnostic. An individualized multimodal management plan emphasized sleep and circadian regularity, Mediterranean-style dietary measures, hydration, gradual aerobic and resistance exercise, cognitive and social engagement, and nonprescription nutritional supplementation without psychotropic medication. Over approximately six months, the patient and his wife reported improvement in memory, attention, organization, communication, motivation, and overall cognitive clarity, accompanied by renewed reading and cycling activity. Repeat SAGE increased by 9 points, from 9/22 to 18/22. Because several interventions were implemented concurrently, no single treatment component can be assigned a causal effect, and spontaneous improvement, natural variability, regression toward the mean, and practice effects cannot be excluded as contributors to the observed change. This case suggests that meaningful cognitive improvement may occur during individualized, multimodal longitudinal care while underscoring the importance of repeated reassessment and cautious interpretation of adjunctive brain perfusion SPECT.

papers.title: Characterizing Cancer Symptom Experiences and Related Psychosocial Concerns Through Chinese Social Media Narratives: Computational Text Analysis.
papers.abstract: Patients with cancer frequently experience complex and multidimensional symptom burdens. Standardized patient-reported outcome measures provide structured approaches to symptom assessment but may not capture the full range of symptom-related and psychosocial concerns expressed in patients' narratives. Patient-generated social media data offer a complementary source for examining how these concerns are expressed online. This study aimed to characterize cancer symptom-related narratives in Chinese social media posts using a conventional symptom assessment framework and to identify additional experiential themes through neural topic modeling. A computational text analysis integrating large language model (LLM) annotation and neural topic modeling was conducted. A corpus of 26,086 first-person patient narratives was collected from Xiaohongshu and Zhihu between November 2013 and February 2026 using cancer-related search terms. First-person narratives and 6 SPPADE (sleep disturbance, pain, physical function impairment, anxiety, depression, and low energy or fatigue) symptom domains were identified using GPT-4o-mini (OpenAI) and validated against independent human coding. Symptom occurrence, co-occurrence, multiplicity, and coping strategies were characterized, with exploratory stratified analyses by cancer type. BERTopic modeling was applied to identify latent themes, platform sensitivity analyses, and temporal distribution were examined. For first-person narrative identification, human raters showed 89.2% agreement (Cohen κ=0.784); the LLM achieved an F1-score of 81.2% against the adjudicated reference standard. For SPPADE extraction, mean Cohen κ values for LLM-human agreement were 0.714 (SD 0.114) and 0.754 (SD 0.095) across the 6 symptom domains. Overall, 13,896 of 26,086 (53.3%) posts contained at least 1 identifiable symptom. Pain was the most frequently identified symptom (5783/26,086, 22.2%), followed by physical function impairment (4153/26,086, 15.9%) and depression (4050/26,086, 15.5%). Pain and physical function impairment formed the most frequent co-occurring symptom pair (n=1407). Coping strategies were described in 7104/26,086 (27.2%) posts; medication-based approaches were most prominent, particularly for pain and sleep disturbance, while social and psychological support were more common for anxiety and depression. BERTopic modeling identified 13 latent themes, including cancer treatment trajectories, health care system interaction, existential distress, family involvement, and financial burden, highlighting experiential concerns that may be underrepresented in conventional symptom assessment. The proportion of posts containing at least 1 SPPADE symptom was similar between Xiaohongshu and Zhihu (53.2% vs 54.1%; P=.35), although individual symptom distributions differed across platforms. Chinese social media posts contained multidimensional symptom-related narratives alongside psychosocial and experiential concerns that may be less visible in structured symptom assessment. Patient-generated social media data may therefore provide a complementary source for understanding cancer symptom experiences and supportive care concerns. However, differences in platform composition, uneven temporal coverage, and the nonrepresentativeness of social media users limit generalizability, and the clinical utility of integrating such data into routine symptom assessment requires further evaluation.

papers.title: Unilateral nonarteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy associated with obstructive sleep apnea-hypopnea syndrome: a case report.
papers.abstract: This report describes a case of obstructive sleep apnea-hypopnea syndrome (OSAHS) associated with nonarteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy (NAION). NAION is an optic neuropathy characterized by painless vision loss, visual field defects, and optic disc edema. It results from hypoperfusion of the short posterior ciliary arteries, leading to acute ischemia and structural and functional impairment of the optic nerve, which ultimately manifests as blurred vision or blindness. We report the case of a 59-year-old Han Chinese male who presented with a 6-day history of blurred vision and visual field defects in the left eye. The diagnosis was confirmed after excluding other potential etiologies. The patient was treated with 80 mg of oral methylprednisolone, which was gradually tapered, alongside neuroprotective and circulation-improving therapies. Following consultation with the Department of Respiratory and Sleep Medicine, he was initiated on noninvasive ventilation (NIV) to correct systemic hypoxia and received bronchodilators. Subsequently, the patient's symptoms showed moderate improvement. NAION is frequently associated with a variety of systemic vascular risk factors, particularly hypertension, diabetes mellitus, dyslipidemia, ischemic heart disease, and cerebrovascular disease. These conditions compromise the microvascular supply to the optic nerve head, leading to ischemia, necrosis, and subsequent optic atrophy. Among these, OSAHS is recognized as a significant and independent risk factor. OSAHS is a clinical syndrome characterized by recurrent episodes of apnea and hypopnea during sleep, resulting in intermittent hypoxia, hypercapnia, and sleep fragmentation. OSAHS is a well-established risk factor for systemic vascular comorbidities, including cardiovascular disease and diabetes mellitus. In the present case, an association between OSAHS and NAION was observed after excluding other potential confounding etiologies. These findings highlight the clinical importance of screening for and managing OSAHS in patients with NAION, providing a rationale for optimized therapeutic strategies.

papers.title: Rotigotine transdermal patch in Parkinson's disease: a narrative review of pharmacology, clinical evidence, special-population management, and health economics.
papers.abstract: Parkinson's disease (PD) requires lifelong dopaminergic therapy, yet oral routes are frequently compromised by gastrointestinal dysfunction, dysphagia, and perioperative fasting. Abrupt withdrawal of oral dopaminergic drugs may precipitate severe motor deterioration or parkinsonism-hyperpyrexia syndrome. Rotigotine transdermal patch delivers 24-h continuous dopaminergic stimulation (CDS) via a non-ergot dopamine agonist (DA) formulation that bypasses first-pass metabolism and gastrointestinal absorption, and may be particularly useful when oral dopaminergic delivery becomes unreliable or is not possible. To synthesize published evidence on rotigotine pharmacology, clinical efficacy, management in vulnerable populations, safety, real-world effectiveness, and health economics, with emphasis on the incremental contribution of a scenario-based, Asia/China-inclusive, and pharmacy-oriented narrative relative to prior general reviews. Narrative review of randomized controlled trials, meta-analyses, regulatory documents, pharmacoeconomic models, and prospective observational studies identified through structured literature search and bibliographic screening. Transdermal bioavailability is approximately 37% versus less than 5% for oral rotigotine. Pivotal Chinese trials SP0914 (early PD: UPDRS II + III -4.9 vs. -0.2) and SP1037 (advanced PD: placebo-adjusted off-time reduction -1.20 h/d [95% CI -1.83 to -0.57]; within-group change -2.36 h/d) demonstrated efficacy; meta-analyses support motor and selected non-motor benefits, including sleep, mood, and gastrointestinal tolerability, whereas swallowing-related signals remain preliminary and based mainly on small observational studies. Perioperative fasting, dysphagia, end-stage disease, and hepatorenal impairment represent clinically important scenarios in which non-oral delivery may be considered, although supporting evidence outside pivotal motor trials is often limited. Application-site reactions (ASRs) are the principal local adverse events; structured 14-day site rotation reduced ASR from 50.0% to 20.3% (P = 0.0373). Chinese cost-effectiveness analyses reported an incremental cost-effectiveness ratio of 1,118,617.81 CNY per quality-adjusted life year versus pramipexole immediate-release at market price, with price-sensitivity thresholds of 28.5% and 9.5% reductions. Rotigotine provides CDS for patients with PD when oral delivery is unreliable; individualized patient selection, structured pharmaceutical care, and updated pharmacoeconomic evaluation are warranted.

papers.title: Outcomes and Complications of Monobloc Versus Le Fort III Procedures for Treating Craniosynostosis: A Literature Review.
papers.abstract: Craniosynostosis is a congenital disorder resulting in the early fusion of several bones in the skull, causing a deformity of the head and facial structures. The 2 most commonly performed surgical procedures to treat craniosynostosis include the monobloc and Le Fort III procedures. This literature review compares the functional and anatomical outcomes and complications between the monobloc and Le Fort III procedures for treating craniosynostosis. A PubMed search was conducted to identify studies assessing the outcomes following monobloc and Le Fort procedures. Data on anatomical changes, ophthalmic, airway, and neurological sequelae, as well as miscellaneous infectious or aesthetic complications were extracted from each study. A total of 63 articles were included for analysis. The average length of midface advancement across distraction and nondistraction procedures was significantly higher in the monobloc cases (14.28 mm; 98.8% of patients with distraction) compared with Le Fort III cases (12.26 mm; 63% of patients with distraction) (P = 0.002). Both procedures exhibited similar rates of obstructive sleep apnea improvement. Cerebrospinal fluid leakage (69 of 373 monobloc patients; 15 of 448 Le Fort III patients) (P ≤ 0.001), seizures (8 of 373 monobloc surgery patients), and meningitis (9 of 373 and 2 of 448, monobloc and Le Fort III patients respectively) (P = 0.01) were observed. In summary, this review demonstrates that both the monobloc and Le Fort III procedures are effective in producing maxillofacial advancement and correcting craniosynostosis, with the monobloc procedure demonstrating significantly greater average advancement. Future research should investigate the comparison of aesthetic and obstructive sleep apnea outcomes further.

papers.title: Parental Health Information Needs, Child-Health Literacy, and Use of Generative AI Among Parents of Children Aged 0 to 4 Years in France: A Cross-Sectional Study
papers.abstract: Background: The first thousand days are a sensitive window for child health and social health inequalities. When routine care falls short, parents of young children turn to online sources and, recently, to generative artificial intelligence (AI). Evidence on their concerns, child-health literacy, and AI use is scarce. Objective: To describe health informational needs and concerns, child-health literacy, and use of AI for child-health questions, including differences by parental role and parity, among parents of young children. Methods: In this cross-sectional study, two anonymous self-administered online questionnaires were disseminated through a digital health application between May 12 and June 11, 2026, to French-speaking parents of at least one child aged 0 to 47 months in France. Questionnaire 1 covered unmet information needs, concerns across 16 topics, perceived intra-couple concordance, and confidence in routine care. Questionnaire 2 covered a four-item child-health literacy quiz and AI use (frequency, topics, 12-month trend, barriers, trust conditions, perceived effect on consultations, and disclosure). Results: In total, 12,634 parents responded (Questionnaire 1, n=5,410; Questionnaire 2, n=7,224), mostly mothers (94.6% and 92.9%). Most (61.8%) had searched for information without finding a clear, reliable answer, selecting a median of 4 (Interquartile range [IQR] 3-7) over 16 topics. Leading concerns were sleep (51.3%), nutrition (48.1%), and education (i.e., upbringing and behavior) (47.8%). Mothers were nearly twice as likely as fathers to select accident prevention (26.5% vs 16.3%) and parental mental health (38.7% vs 28.6%); first-time parents selected most topics more often than experienced parents, most markedly dental hygiene (43.8% vs 27.6%). The median child-health literacy score was 3 (IQR 3-4) on a 0-to-4 quiz, with 19.9% of parents scoring 2 or below; tooth-brushing age was the weakest item (68.4% correct). Mothers outscored fathers on every item. More than half of parents (54.2%) had used AI for a child-health question, 11.2% weekly; among those reporting a trend, 68.3% had increased AI use for child-health questions over the year and 6.2% decreased it. The main barriers to AI use were a preference for professionals (55.9%) and reliability concerns (48.7%); trust depended most on medical oversight of the tool (76.6%). AI use appeared additive, with 66.8% reporting no change in healthcare visit frequency. One third (35.5%) had told an AI something shared with neither a professional nor their network, rising to 64.1% among regular users. Conclusions: Parental informational needs were widespread and frequently unmet. AI has become a common and fast-rising source for child-health questions, at times a confidential one, used alongside rather than instead of professionals. Child-health literacy was generally high but uneven, with oral health the clearest gap. Strengths include the sample size and early-generative-AI timing; limitations include the cross-sectional design, self-report, digital-recruitment selection bias, and the small proportion of fathers.
